During an influenza epidemic, 4% of a population of a large city were affected on a given day. The manager of a factory that employs 250 people found that 17 of the employees at his factory were absent, claiming to be suffering from influenza. Using a Poisson approximation to the binomial distribution and a 5% level of significance, test whether or not the proportion of employees suffering from influenza at his factory was larger than that of the whole city.

Question 11

The number of breakdowns per day in a large fleet of hire cars has a Poisson distribution with mean 0.3. Find the probability that in a 20-day period the number of breakdowns is:\par \textbf{a} exactly 5\par \textbf{b} no more than 8.\par The hire car company introduces new servicing guidelines in order to try to decrease the number of cars that break down. In a randomly chosen 30-day period following the introduction of the new measures, 5 cars break down.\par \textbf{c} Test, at the 5% level of significance, whether or not the mean number of breakdowns has decreased. State your hypotheses clearly.

\textbf{a} Let $X$ count breakdowns in 20 days. $X\sim\mathrm{Po}(20\times0.3)=\mathrm{Po}(6)$.\par $P(X=5)=e^{-6}6^5/5!=0.1606$ (4 d.p.).\par \textbf{b} From the cumulative Poisson tables, $P(X\le 8)=0.8472$.\par \textbf{c} Let $Y$ count breakdowns in 30 days and let $\lambda$ be its mean. $H_0:\lambda=30\times0.3=9$ against $H_1:\lambda<9$.\par Under $H_0$, $Y\sim\mathrm{Po}(9)$. This is a lower-tail test at 5%.\par $P(Y\le5)=0.1157>0.05$. Do not reject $H_0$. There is insufficient evidence that the mean number of breakdowns has decreased.
Question 12

A doctor expects to see, on average, 2.25 patients per week with a particular condition. The doctor decides to send information to her patients to try and reduce the number of patients she sees with the condition. In the first four weeks after the information is sent, she sees 4 patients with the condition. Test at the 5% level of significance, whether or not there is reason to believe that sending the information has reduced the number of times the doctor sees patients with the condition.

Let $X$ count patients with this condition seen in four weeks and let $\lambda$ denote its mean.\par $H_0:\lambda=4\times 2.25=9$ against $H_1:\lambda<9$.\par Under $H_0$, $X\sim\mathrm{Po}(9)$. A reduction gives a lower-tail test at 5%.\par From the tables, $P(X\le4)=0.0550>0.05$.\par Do not reject $H_0$. The observations give insufficient evidence at 5% that sending the information reduced the number of patients seen with the condition.
Question 13

Breakdowns occur on a particular machine at a rate of 1.5 every week. A manager feels that the rate of breakdowns has changed and decides to monitor the machine. Over a 6-week period she finds that there are 13 breakdowns. Test at the 5% level of significance, whether or not the manager’s suspicion is correct.

Let $X$ count breakdowns in six weeks and let $\lambda$ be the six-week mean.\par $H_0:\lambda=6\times1.5=9$ against $H_1:\lambda\ne9$. Under $H_0$, $X\sim\mathrm{Po}(9)$.\par A change in either direction matters. At 5%, allow 2.5% in each tail. The observed 13 is above 9, so use the upper tail.\par $P(X\ge13)=1-P(X\le12)=1-0.8758=0.1242$.\par $0.1242>0.025$. Do not reject $H_0$. There is insufficient evidence that the breakdown rate has changed.
Question 14

A factory produces components, of which 1% are defective. The components are packed in boxes of 1000.\par \textbf{a} Using a Poisson approximation to the binomial distribution, estimate the probability that a randomly chosen box contains:\par (i) exactly 9 defective components\par (ii) no more than 7 defective components.\par \textbf{b} Explain why this approximation is suitable.\par The machinery in the factory is serviced and it is found that in the first box produced following the servicing there are 5 defective components.\par \textbf{c} Is there evidence to suggest at the 5% level of significance that the servicing has reduced the number of defective components? State your hypotheses clearly.

\textbf{a} Let $X$ count defective components in a box. $X\sim\mathrm{B}(1000,0.01)$. Approximate this by $Y\sim\mathrm{Po}(1000\times0.01)=\mathrm{Po}(10)$.\par (i) $P(X=9)\approx P(Y=9)=e^{-10}10^9/9!=0.1251$.\par (ii) From the cumulative tables, $P(X\le7)\approx P(Y\le7)=0.2202$.\par \textbf{b} The number of trials, $n=1000$, is large and the probability of a defect, $p=0.01$, is small.\par \textbf{c} Let $\lambda$ be the mean number of defects per box after servicing. $H_0:\lambda=10$, $H_1:\lambda<10$. Under $H_0$ use $Y\sim\mathrm{Po}(10)$.\par This is a lower-tail test at 5%. $P(Y\le5)=0.0671>0.05$. Do not reject $H_0$. There is insufficient evidence that servicing has reduced the number of defective components.

transcription.tex:
A company claims that it receives emails at a mean rate of 2 every 5 minutes.
(a) Give two reasons why a Poisson distribution could be a suitable model for the number of emails received.
(b) Using a 5% level of significance, find the critical region for a two-tailed test of the hypothesis that the mean number of emails received in a 10 minute period is 4. The probability of rejection in each tail should be as close as possible to 0.025.
(c) Find the actual level of significance of this test.
To test this claim, the number of emails received in a random 10 minute period was recorded.
During this period 8 emails were received.
(d) Comment on the company’s claim in the light of this value. Justify your answer.
Edexcel S2(Old) June 2014 Q3

(a) Any two of the following. Emails arrive independently. They arrive singly. The mean rate is constant.
(b) \(X\sim\operatorname{Po}(4)\). \(P(X=0)=0.0183\) and \(P(X\ge9)=0.0214\).
Critical region: \(X=0\) or \(X\ge9\).

(c) \(0.0183+0.0214=0.0397\), or 3.97%.
(d) 8 is outside the critical region. Equivalently, \(P(X\ge8)=0.0511\). There is insufficient evidence against the company’s claim.

slides.navigationTitle: Exam style question · Edexcel S2(Old) June 2014 Q3

transcription.tex: Question 8

During term time, incoming calls to a school are thought to occur at a rate of 0.25 per minute. To test this, the number of calls during a random 30-minute interval is recorded.\par \textbf{a} Find the critical region for a two-tailed test of the hypothesis that the number of incoming calls occurs at a rate other than 0.25 per minute. The probability in each tail should be as close to 2.5% as possible.\par \textbf{b} Find the actual significance level of the above test.\par The actual number of calls recorded in this 30-minute period was 11.\par \textbf{c} Comment on this observation in light of the critical region.

\textbf{a} Let $X$ count calls in 30 minutes and let $\lambda$ be its mean. $H_0:\lambda=30\times0.25=7.5$, $H_1:\lambda\ne7.5$. Under $H_0$, $X\sim\mathrm{Po}(7.5)$.\par Aim for 0.025 in each tail. At the lower end, $P(X\le2)=0.0203$ and $P(X\le3)=0.0591$. The closer value is 0.0203, so use $X\le2$.\par At the upper end, $P(X\ge13)=1-P(X\le12)=1-0.9573=0.0427$.\par $P(X\ge14)=1-P(X\le13)=1-0.9784=0.0216$. This is closer to 0.025, so use $X\ge14$.\par The critical region is $X\le2$ or $X\ge14$.\par \textbf{b} Actual significance level $=P(X\le2)+P(X\ge14)=0.0203+0.0216=0.0419$, or 4.19%.\par \textbf{c} The observation 11 lies outside this region. Do not reject $H_0$. There is insufficient evidence that the incoming call rate has changed.
Question 9

Millie manufactures printed material. She knows that defects occur randomly in the manufacturing process at a rate of 1 every 7 metres. Once a week the machinery is cleaned and reset. Millie then takes a random sample of 35 metres of material from the next batch produced to test if there has been any change in the rate of defects.\par \textbf{a} Stating your hypotheses clearly and using a 10% level of significance, find the critical region for this test. You should choose your critical region so that the probability of rejection is less than 0.05 in each tail.\par \textbf{b} State the actual significance level of this test.

\textbf{a} Let $X$ count defects in 35 metres and let $\lambda$ be its mean. $H_0:\lambda=35\times\frac17=5$, $H_1:\lambda\ne5$. Under $H_0$, $X\sim\mathrm{Po}(5)$.\par At 10% use less than 0.05 in each tail. $P(X\le1)=0.0404<0.05$, while $P(X\le2)=0.1247>0.05$. The lower region is $X\le1$.\par $P(X\ge9)=1-P(X\le8)=1-0.9319=0.0681>0.05$.\par $P(X\ge10)=1-P(X\le9)=1-0.9682=0.0318<0.05$. The upper region is $X\ge10$.\par The critical region is $X\le1$ or $X\ge10$.\par \textbf{b} Actual significance level $=P(X\le1)+P(X\ge10)=0.0404+0.0318=0.0722$, or 7.22%.
Question 10

A company claims that it receives emails at a mean rate of 3 every 5 minutes.\par \textbf{a} Give two conditions under which a Poisson distribution would be a suitable model for the number of emails received.\par To test its claim, the company records the number of emails received in a 15-minute period.\par \textbf{b} Using a 5% level of significance, find the critical region for a two-tailed test of the hypothesis that the mean number of emails received in a 15-minute period is different from 9. The probability of rejection in each tail should be as close as possible to 0.025.\par \textbf{c} Find the actual level of significance of this test.\par The actual number of emails received in this period was 13.\par \textbf{d} Comment on the company’s claim in the light of this value. Justify your answer.

\textbf{a} Emails arrive independently and at random at a constant average rate.\par \textbf{b} Let $X$ count emails in 15 minutes. Its mean is $\lambda$. Test $H_0:\lambda=3\times3=9$ against $H_1:\lambda\ne9$. Under $H_0$, $X\sim\mathrm{Po}(9)$.\par Aim for 0.025 in each tail. $P(X\le3)=0.0212$ and $P(X\le4)=0.0550$. The closer value gives $X\le3$.\par $P(X\ge15)=1-P(X\le14)=1-0.9585=0.0415$.\par $P(X\ge16)=1-P(X\le15)=1-0.9780=0.0220$. The closer value gives $X\ge16$. The critical region is $X\le3$ or $X\ge16$.\par \textbf{c} Actual significance level $=P(X\le3)+P(X\ge16)=0.0212+0.0220=0.0432$, or 4.32%.\par \textbf{d} The observed 13 falls outside the critical region. Do not reject $H_0$. There is insufficient evidence that the mean differs from 9 per 15 minutes, or 3 every 5 minutes.
Question 11

A single observation $x$ is to be taken from a Poisson distribution with parameter $\lambda$. This observation is to be used to test, at a 5% level of significance, $H_0:\lambda=c$ against $H_1:\lambda\ne c$, where $c$ is a positive integer. The probability in each tail is less than 0.025. Given that the critical region for this test is $X\le 2$ or $X\ge 15$,\par \textbf{a} find the value of $c$, justifying your answer.\par \textbf{b} Find the actual significance level of this test.

\textbf{a} Consider the lower tail first. From the Poisson tables, $P(X\le2)=0.0296$ at $\lambda=7$ and $0.0138$ at $\lambda=8$.\par Increasing the mean reduces this lower-tail probability. For the probability to be below 0.025 we need $c\ge8$.\par Now consider $P(X\ge15)=1-P(X\le14)$. At $\lambda=9$ this is $1-0.9585=0.0415$. At $\lambda=8$ it is $1-0.9827=0.0173$.\par Increasing the mean increases this upper-tail probability. We need $c\le8$. The only positive integer meeting both conditions is $c=8$.\par \textbf{b} Actual significance level $=P(X\le2)+P(X\ge15)=0.0138+0.0173=0.0311$, or 3.11%.

transcription.tex: Question 8

On average Lucy scores a goal in one of every 4 attempts from a free kick.\par \textbf{a} State a suitable distribution to model the number of attempts needed to score her first goal.\par \textbf{b} Find the probability that she scores her first goal on her 5th attempt.\par After an injury, Lucy scores her first goal from a free kick on her 10th attempt.\par \textbf{c} Test, at the 5% level of significance, whether the probability of her scoring a goal from a free kick is now less than $\frac{1}{4}$.

\textbf{a} Let $X$ be the number of free kicks up to and including Lucy's first goal. $X\sim\mathrm{Geo}(0.25)$.\par \textbf{b} For a first goal on the fifth attempt there must be four misses and then a goal. $P(X=5)=(1-0.25)^4(0.25)=0.0791$ (4 d.p.).\par \textbf{c} Let $p$ be the probability of a goal on each kick after the injury. $H_0:p=0.25$, $H_1:p<0.25$. Under $H_0$, $X\sim\mathrm{Geo}(0.25)$.\par A lower success probability means a longer wait. For 10 or more attempts the first nine must be misses: $P(X\ge10)=(1-0.25)^9=0.0751$.\par $0.0751>0.05$. Do not reject $H_0$. There is insufficient evidence that Lucy's probability of scoring is now less than $\frac14$.
Question 11

Marie claims that she scores a penalty on 30% of her attempts. One of her rivals claims that she is overstating her ability. In an attempt to prove her case, Marie takes consecutive shots until she scores her first penalty. She scores her first penalty on her 10th shot. Test her rival’s claim, using a 5% level of significance and clearly stating your null and alternative hypotheses.

Let $X$ count penalties up to and including Marie's first goal. Let $p$ be her probability of scoring each penalty.\par $H_0:p=0.3$, $H_1:p<0.3$. Under $H_0$, $X\sim\mathrm{Geo}(0.3)$. Use a one-tailed test at 5%.\par The rival predicts a longer wait. Ten or more attempts means missing at least the first nine.\par $P(X\ge10)=(1-0.3)^9=0.0404$ (4 d.p.).\par $0.0404<0.05$. Reject $H_0$. There is sufficient evidence at 5% to support the rival's claim that Marie is overstating her ability.
Question 12

Imelda is a bird watcher. The probability that she will see a robin on any given day is $\frac{1}{6}$.\par The random variable $X$ represents the number of days until Imelda first sees a robin.\par \textbf{a} Write down a suitable distribution to model $X$, and give two conditions that are necessary for this model to be valid.\par \textbf{b} Calculate the probability that Imelda sees her first robin\par (i) on the third day\par (ii) after the fourth day.\par Imelda further claims that the probability that she will see a magpie on any given day is $\frac{1}{4}$. It is decided to test Imelda’s claim. It is found from her records that it took 12 days until she saw her first magpie.\par \textbf{c} Is there any evidence at the 5% level of significance that Imelda is overstating the probability of seeing a magpie on any given day? State your hypotheses clearly.

\textbf{a} $X\sim\mathrm{Geo}(\frac16)$. The probability of seeing a robin stays constant each day, and sightings on different days are independent.\par \textbf{b} (i) Two days without a robin and then a sighting give $P(X=3)=(1-\frac16)^2\frac16=0.1157$.\par (ii) Four days without a robin give $P(X>4)=P(X\ge5)=(1-\frac16)^4=0.4823$.\par \textbf{c} Let $p$ be the daily magpie sighting probability and $Y$ the wait for the first magpie. $H_0:p=0.25$, $H_1:p<0.25$. Under $H_0$, $Y\sim\mathrm{Geo}(0.25)$.\par A wait of 12 or more days means no magpie for the first 11 days. $P(Y\ge12)=(1-0.25)^{11}=0.0422$.\par $0.0422<0.05$. Reject $H_0$. There is sufficient evidence at 5% that Imelda is overstating the probability of seeing a magpie on any given day.

For this particularly scenario, each ‘trial’ has two outcomes, so
we could have either done this Geometric test, or a Binomial test
by doing a fixed number of trials and counting how many times the card is rejected.
Why would a Geometric test be better in this scenario?

Because the probability of a card being rejected is very low, we would have to have a very large number of trials in order to see any card failures. A geometric test therefore requires fewer trials, as only one card failure is required.
